headline: Yale scientists may have found a shortcut to the anti-aging benefits of eating less

paragraphs.text: Yale scientists may have uncovered a shortcut to achieving some of the anti-aging benefits of eating less without having to restrict calories. Their discovery centers on an immune system protein that helps protect the body from infections but may also contribute to chronic inflammation as we grow older.

Reducing calorie intake has been shown to extend lifespan in several animal species, including mice, rhesus monkeys, and fruit flies. In some cases, these animals also remain free of disease for longer. However, extreme calorie restriction can come at a significant biological cost. Mice that consume 40% fewer calories, for example, become more vulnerable to infections, experience impaired growth, and are less likely to reproduce.

Researchers have long sought a way to harness the potential longevity benefits of calorie restriction in humans without these harmful consequences. In a new study published in Nature Aging, Yale scientists identified a promising target: an immune system protein known as complement component 3 (C3).

Earlier research from Yale demonstrated that people who reduced their calorie intake by a moderate 14% over two years experienced improvements in immune defense without sacrificing growth or reproductive function.

"This concept demonstrates that aging is actually malleable and a process that can be targeted," says senior author Vishwa Deep Dixit, PhD, Waldemar Von Zedtwitz Professor of Pathology, professor of immunobiology and of comparative medicine, and director of the Yale Center for Research on Aging (Y-Age) at Yale School of Medicine.
Eating Less Reduces a Protein Linked to Aging

For their latest investigation, Dixit and his colleagues at Yale School of Medicine examined blood plasma samples from 42 participants in a two-year clinical trial funded by the National Institutes of Health. The trial, known as CALERIE, stands for Comprehensive Assessment of Long-Term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy.
"It's the only trial of its kind that has been done with such rigor and control and demonstrates relevance to human physiology," Dixit says.
Over the course of the trial, participants successfully lowered their calorie consumption by 11% to 14% without experiencing a sense of deprivation.

By examining blood samples collected over time, the scientists identified more than 7,000 proteins. One particularly intriguing finding was that levels of C3 fell significantly in response to calorie restriction.

C3 is a central component of the complement system, a network of proteins that helps the immune system recognize and eliminate potentially harmful invaders, including bacteria. Although this system is essential for protecting the body, excessive activation may have damaging consequences.

Previous research has linked complement system activity to chronic inflammation, a persistent inflammatory response that can damage healthy tissues over time. Chronic inflammation is considered a major hallmark of biological aging and contributes to the development of numerous age-related diseases.

"But the causal effects of C3 in aging and chronic inflammation have not been identified. So, we were very excited to find that in our study," says Hee-Hoon Kim, PhD, a postdoctoral associate in the Dixit lab and a co-first author of the paper.
A Surprising Discovery Hidden in Body Fat

By comparing protein levels at the beginning and end of the two-year calorie restriction period, the researchers pinpointed white adipose tissue as the primary tissue affected by the dietary intervention. White adipose tissue is the most abundant type of body fat in mammals. Beyond storing energy, it plays important roles in metabolism, hormone production, and immune function.
The researchers then turned to mice to investigate the biological mechanisms behind their findings. Consistent with observations in humans, C3 expression increased as the animals aged.

Further biochemical experiments revealed an unexpected source of this increase: visceral white adipose tissue. Visceral fat accumulates deep within the abdomen, surrounding internal organs, and has been associated with chronic inflammation and metabolic disease.
"We were not expecting that because these proteins are mainly synthesized in the liver," says Manish Mishra, PhD, a postdoctoral associate in the Dixit lab and a co-first author of the study.

Using a technique called single-cell RNA sequencing, which allows scientists to examine gene activity within individual cells, the team traced the production of C3 to specific populations of macrophages associated with aging that reside within fat tissue.
"This whole process was unknown in the beginning," Mishra says. "Just to narrow it down to the subtypes of macrophages responsible for this complement protein production was very challenging."

Macrophages are white blood cells that form part of the body's first line of immune defense. They are best known for surrounding, engulfing, and destroying potentially harmful microorganisms. However, as Dixit explains, they also perform essential functions that help maintain healthy tissues and keep biological processes in balance.
Anti-Aging Benefits May Be Independent of Weight Loss
The discovery raised an important question: Could people benefit from lower C3 activity without having to lose weight?
Initially, the scientists suspected that losing body fat through calorie restriction might reduce the production of C3 and help counter some of the biological processes associated with aging.
There was good reason to suspect a connection. Most participants in the clinical trial lost about 18 pounds during two years of moderate calorie restriction.
However, when the team examined changes in participants' body mass index, they found no correlation between weight loss and reductions in complement protein levels.
"This suggests that calorie restriction has a beneficial effect that is unique to adipose tissues and is likely independent of weight loss," Kim says.

The researchers also tested whether a drug could reproduce this particular benefit of calorie restriction. When they pharmacologically inhibited C3 activation in mice, the animals experienced a reduction in age-related inflammation.

Although the experiments did not establish that blocking C3 extends lifespan or slows aging in humans, they suggest that targeting this protein could reproduce some of the beneficial biological effects of eating less.
When the Immune System Turns Against the Body
According to Dixit, the findings illustrate an important principle in aging research: Biological processes that benefit us when we are young can become harmful later in life.

This idea, known as antagonistic pleiotropy, has its conceptual roots in evolutionary theories of aging developed by biologist Peter Medawar in 1952. The theory of antagonistic pleiotropy was subsequently formalized by evolutionary biologist George C. Williams in 1957.
One example is growth hormone, which is essential for normal growth and development during childhood but may also contribute to the development of cancer later in life.

A similar trade-off may occur with proteins such as C3. Throughout human evolution, these molecules have played a vital role in protecting people from potentially deadly infections. However, as humans increasingly live to advanced ages, excessive activity of these same protective mechanisms may contribute to chronic inflammation and declining health.
Dixit suggests that reducing C3 levels could offer a way to extend health span, the portion of a person's life spent in good health, rather than simply increasing the number of years they live.
Could Existing Drugs Mimic Calorie Restriction?

The Yale team is now investigating whether FDA-approved complement inhibitor drugs could be used to counter the harmful effects of excessive C3 activity and potentially slow aspects of aging in humans.
The challenge will be to reduce damaging inflammation without compromising the immune system's ability to protect the body from infections.
"The idea is not to remove complement systems that are required for us to fight infections," Dixit says. "Instead, the goal is to restore the balance."
